card.name: Charleston
card.tagline: New York, 1923 — knees in, knees out, the dance that defined the Roaring Twenties.
card.profile: The Charleston is a dance named after the harbor city of Charleston, South Carolina. The rhythm was popularized in mainstream dance music in the United States by a 1923 tune called "The Charleston" by composer/pianist James P. Johnson, which originated in the Broadway show Runnin' Wild and became one of the most popular hits of the decade. Runnin' Wild ran from 28 October 1923 through 28 June 1924. The Charleston dance's peak popularity occurred from mid-1926 to 1927.
card.insight: The Guinness World Record for the largest Charleston dance is 1,096 participants, set by Revel In Dance in Shrewsbury, UK, on September 22, 2018. parts.note: Welcoming students and introducing the Charleston steps.
Demonstrating the pattern of the basic Charleston step from the back.

steps.name: Basic Charleston step
steps.description: Step back and touch with bounce and opposite arm movement.

steps.name: Charleston Kicks
steps.description: Swinging kicks replacing steps with wider, groovier movement.

steps.name: Kick Step
steps.description: Holding and kicking then stepping where you kicked.

steps.name: Charleston with Twist
steps.description: Twisting on heels with the weight on balls of feet.

images: Imagine that you're dancing on a hot frying pan
common_mistakes: Leaning upper body backward instead of keeping continuous body position to the front
lessons.teacher_style: The teacher explains steps clearly with enthusiasm and provides multiple variations. She uses counting and verbal rhythm to guide students through posture and footwork.
lessons.distinctive_method: Categorizing Charleston variations into distinct stylistic eras like '20s style', 'Savoy swing style', and 'Afro twist' to explain posture and movement quality differences.
what_works: Demonstrating from behind helps mirror footwork easily
Clear verbal cues matched to rhythm
what_hinders: Rapid transitions between multiple variations without much repetition

evidence.observation: Teacher demonstrates basic Charleston footwork facing away from the camera, counting 5-6-7-8 while stepping back and touching.

evidence.cannot_infer: exact muscular tension in the arms

evidence.observation: Teacher demonstrates back and front kicks with heel shakes from a rear angle.
